title: Adjectives and adverbs; good and well; comparisons
blurb: Choose adjective or adverb (good or well, bad or badly, real or really) and form comparatives and superlatives correctly.
question: An applicant's essay says, “I felt real tired, but I still did good on my shift. Of the three clinical sites, this one was the better, and the staff treated me more kinder than at the others.” What is wrong, and how should it read?

teach.h: Adjectives describe things; adverbs describe actions and qualities
teach.body: Formally, an adjective modifies a noun or pronoun, and an adverb modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb. Plain English: ask what the word describes. If it describes a person or thing (a careful nurse), use the adjective. If it describes how, when or how much something is done (works carefully, really tired), use the adverb. The HESI A2 gives you the wrong one and checks whether you notice.

head: Type
Modifies
Example
rows: a careful nurse; she is quick
a really high fever (not real high)
The milk smells sour. I feel tired.
teach.caption: Linking verbs (be, seem, become, feel, look, taste, smell, sound) connect the subject to an adjective that describes it.

teach.h: After the verb: adjective or adverb?

root.label: Does the word describe the subject or the action?

children.label: Linking verb: adjective
children.sub: The soup tastes salty. She looks tired.

children.label: Action verb: adverb
children.sub: She tasted it carefully. He looked closely.

teach.caption: Same verb, two jobs: “She looked tired” (linking) vs “She looked carefully at the rash” (action).

teach.body: Good is an adjective: “a good result,” “The food tastes good.” Well is an adverb: “She did well on the exam,” “The wound is healing well.” Well is also an adjective meaning healthy: “I feel well today.” So after an action verb (did, slept, healed, works, performed) the answer is well. After a linking verb, good describes quality and well describes health.

teach.h: Bad vs badly, real vs really
teach.caption: “Real” as an adverb (real good, real tired) is informal; formal writing uses “really.”

teach.h: Comparing two vs three or more
head: Base
Two things
Three or more
teach.caption: One-syllable words add -er/-est; most words of three or more syllables use more/most. Never both: not “more busier,” not “most worst.”

teach.body: Nursing applicant Tyler Nguyen wrote: “I felt real tired, but I still did good on my shift. Of the three clinical sites, this one was the better, and the staff treated me more kinder than at the others.” “Real” modifies the adjective “tired,” so “really tired.” “Did” is an action verb, so “did well.” Three sites call for the superlative: “the best.” “More kinder” is a double comparison and should describe an action: “treated me more kindly.”

teach.text: HESI A2 traps: “did good,” “real tired,” “tastes badly” after a linking verb, “the better of the three,” and double comparisons such as “more busier” or “most worst.” Also beware -ly adjectives (friendly, lonely, costly): they describe nouns, so they are not adverbs.

items: Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.
Linking verbs take adjectives (tastes salty, sounds bad); action verbs take adverbs (did well, slept badly).
Good is an adjective; well is an adverb, or an adjective meaning healthy.
Really, not real, before an adjective in formal writing (really tired).
Two things: -er or more; three or more: -est or most; never both together.
Irregular: good/well, better, best; bad/badly, worse, worst.

summary: You can now choose adjectives after linking verbs and adverbs after action verbs, including good or well, bad or badly and real or really. You can also form comparatives for two items and superlatives for three or more without doubling up.

A.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “The patient said she feels ___ today, and her incision is healing ___.”
A.why: “Well” as an adjective means healthy after the linking verb “feels,” and “well” as an adverb modifies the action verb “healing.”

whyNot.0: “Healing” is an action verb and needs the adverb “well,” not the adjective “good.”
whyNot.1: “Healing good” is wrong: action verbs take adverbs.
whyNot.3: “Feels” is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective; “nicely” is an adverb.

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Of the three practice tests, the second one was the ___.”
A.why: Three items call for the superlative. “Hard” is one syllable, so it takes -est: “hardest.”

whyNot.0: “Harder” is the comparative, used for two items, not three.
whyNot.1: One-syllable adjectives add -est rather than using “most.”
whyNot.3: “More harder” is a double comparison, and it is also the comparative form.

A.q: In the sentence “The new aide answered the phone politely,” which word is an adverb?
A.why: “Politely” tells how the aide answered, so it modifies the verb and is an adverb.

whyNot.0: “New” describes the noun “aide,” so it is an adjective.
whyNot.3: “Phone” is a noun, the direct object.

B.q: Which sentence uses adjectives and adverbs correctly?
options: The new graduate did real good on her first review.
The cough syrup tastes badly, but it works quickly.
She charted careful so the next shift could follow.
The rash looks worse today than it did yesterday.
B.why: “Looks” is a linking verb, so it takes an adjective; “worse” is the correct comparative of “bad” for two days.

whyNot.0: “Real” should be the adverb “really,” and “did good” should be “did well.”
whyNot.1: “Tastes” is a linking verb and takes an adjective: “tastes bad.”
whyNot.2: “Charted” is an action verb and needs the adverb “carefully.”

B.q: Which sentence about two nursing programs is correct?
options: Of the two programs, Riverside is the best choice.
Of the two programs, Riverside is the more better choice.
Of the two programs, Riverside is the most affordable.
Of the two programs, Riverside is the better choice.
B.why: Two programs call for the comparative “better.”

whyNot.0: “Best” is the superlative, for three or more.
whyNot.2: “Most affordable” is the superlative; with two programs use “more affordable.”

B.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The patient's fever was ___ high when she arrived at the clinic.”
B.why: “High” is an adjective, and only an adverb can modify an adjective: “dangerously high.”

whyNot.0: “Dangerous” is an adjective and cannot modify another adjective.
whyNot.2: “Danger” is a noun and cannot modify an adjective.
whyNot.3: “Dangerousness” is a noun and cannot modify an adjective.

options: The burn on his hand looked bad this morning.
The intern wrote the order bad and had to fix it.
The patient slept bad because of the hallway noise.
The child scraped his knee bad on the playground.
C.why: “Looked” is a linking verb here: it links the burn to a description, so the adjective “bad” is correct.

whyNot.1: “Wrote” is an action verb and needs the adverb “badly.”
whyNot.2: “Slept” is an action verb and needs the adverb “badly.”
whyNot.3: “Scraped” is an action verb and needs the adverb “badly.”

C.q: Which sentence uses a comparison correctly?
options: This is the most easiest dosage chart to read.
Of all the units, the ICU is the busiest at night.
Of the twins, Maya is the tallest by two inches.
The new monitor is more quieter than the old one.
C.why: “Of all the units” compares three or more, so the superlative “busiest” is correct.

whyNot.0: “Most easiest” is a double superlative; use “easiest.”
whyNot.2: Twins are two people, so the comparative “taller” is needed.
whyNot.3: “More quieter” is a double comparative; use “quieter.”

C.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “The soup smelled ___, so Dev stirred it ___ before serving it.”
C.why: “Smelled” is a linking verb here, so it takes the adjective “good”; “stirred” is an action verb, so it takes the adverb “carefully.”

whyNot.0: “Stirred” is an action verb and needs the adverb “carefully.”
whyNot.1: After the linking verb “smelled,” describing the soup's quality needs the adjective “good.”
whyNot.3: “Goodly” means large in amount, and “stirred” needs the adverb “carefully.”

reteach.title: Labels on jars, notes on actions
reteach.question: Picture a supply room: every jar has a label describing what is inside, and every task card has a note describing how to do the task. Which kind of word goes on which?

blocks.body: A jar label describes the thing: sterile gauze, large gloves, a good batch. That is an adjective's job. A task note describes the doing: wrap firmly, check often, work well. That is an adverb's job. Linking verbs are the glass of the jar: “The gauze is sterile,” “The batch looks good.” They point back to the thing, so the label word (an adjective) follows them.

blocks.text: A word that ends in -ly is not always a task note: “a friendly aide” and “a costly repair” are jar labels (adjectives).

explain.body: Ask what the word describes. A person or thing takes an adjective; an action, a quality or another adverb takes an adverb.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The nurse checked the IV line ___ before starting the infusion.”
test.why: The word tells how she checked, so it modifies the action verb and must be the adverb “carefully.”

whyNot.0: “Careful” is an adjective; it cannot describe the action “checked.”
whyNot.2: “Carefuller” is not a standard form, and the sentence needs an adverb.
whyNot.3: “More careful” is a comparative adjective, and nothing is being compared.

explain.body: Feel, look, seem, taste, smell, sound and become usually link the subject to a description. The description is an adjective: “feel bad,” “looks good,” “sounds bad.”

test.q: Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after a linking verb?
options: The patient's voice sounded hoarse this morning.
The aide spoke rude to the angry visitor.
The waiting room seemed quietly after lunch.
The fresh bandage felt tightly around his wrist.
test.why: “Sounded” links the voice to a description, so the adjective “hoarse” is correct.

whyNot.1: “Spoke” is an action verb and needs the adverb “rudely.”
whyNot.2: “Seemed” is a linking verb, so it takes the adjective “quiet.”
whyNot.3: “Felt” links the bandage to a description, so it takes the adjective “tight.”

explain.body: Good is an adjective. Well is an adverb after action verbs, and an adjective only when it means healthy.

test.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? “I don't feel ___ today, and I didn't sleep ___ last night.”
test.why: “Feel well” (healthy) uses well as an adjective; “sleep well” uses well as an adverb with the action verb “sleep.”

whyNot.1: “Sleep” is an action verb and needs the adverb “well,” not “good.”
whyNot.2: “Sleep good” is wrong: action verbs take adverbs.
whyNot.3: “Feel” is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective; “nicely” is an adverb.

explain.body: Use -er or more for two things and -est or most for three or more, never both together. Good, well, bad and badly are irregular.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Of the four wound dressings, the silicone one was the ___ to remove.”
test.why: Four items call for the superlative: “least painful.”

whyNot.0: “Less painful” is the comparative, for two items only.
whyNot.2: “Lesser” means smaller in importance (a lesser concern); it does not form comparisons of adjectives.
